section.title: My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me
section.sectionRationale: The crucifixion psalm, its opening cry quoted word for word by Jesus from the cross, Matthew 27:46, and its middle verses describing mocking, thirst, pierced hands and feet, and divided garments with startling precision centuries before crucifixion existed as a punishment. It moves from the deepest possible cry of abandonment to a sweeping vision of worldwide praise, a movement from dereliction to global worship that mirrors the movement from Good Friday to the great commission.
section.thesis: David's cry of abandonment and his enemies' vivid, specific mockery and violence describe, with uncanny precision, the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, whose suffering in forsakenness gives way, just as this psalm does, to a worldwide declaration of God's praise to a people yet unborn.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the opening cry of abandonment against the backdrop of the fathers' trust; the vivid description of mockery, physical agony, and surrounding enemies; the specific details of pierced hands and feet and divided garments; and the closing turn to worldwide praise and proclamation to generations yet unborn.

verses.text: My God, my God, why have You {{azab|forsaken}} me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning?
I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer, and by night, but I have no rest.
Yet You are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel.
In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them.
They cried out to You and were set free; they trusted in You and were not disappointed.
But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people.
All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads:
“He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.”
Yet You brought me forth from the womb; You made me secure at my mother's breast.
From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother's womb You have been my God.

units.label: My strength is dried up like a potsherd

verses.text:
Be not far from me, for trouble is near 
and there is no one to help.
Many bulls surround me; strong bulls of Bashan encircle me.
They open their jaws against me like lions that roar and maul.
I am poured out like water, and all my bones are disjointed. My heart is like wax; it melts away within me.

My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. 
You lay me in the dust of death.

units.label: They have pierced my hands and feet

verses.text:
For dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me; 
they have {{karah|pierced}} my hands and feet.
I can count all my bones; they stare and gloat over me.
They divide my garments among them and cast {{goral|lots}} for my clothing.
But You, O LORD, be not far off; O my Strength, come quickly to help me.
Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.
Save me from the mouth of the lion; at the horns of the wild oxen You have answered me!

units.label: All the ends of the earth will remember

verses.text: I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly.

You who fear the LORD, praise Him! All descendants of Jacob, honor Him! 
All offspring of Israel, revere Him!
For He has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.
My praise for You resounds in the great assembly; I will fulfill my vows before those who fear You.

The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek the LORD will praise Him. 
May your hearts live forever!
All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD. All the families of the nations will bow down before Him.
For dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations.
All the rich of the earth will feast and worship; all who go down to the dust will kneel before Him, even those unable to preserve their lives.
Posterity will serve Him; they will declare the Lord to a new generation.

They will come and proclaim His righteousness to a people yet unborn, 
all that He has done.

azab.gloss: To forsake, abandon, leave. This is the exact word Jesus cries out from the cross in Aramaic, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani, Matthew 27:46, quoting this psalm's opening cry as He bears the weight of sin in our place.

karah.gloss: Pierced, a difficult but well attested reading of the Hebrew text, rendered by ancient translations including the Septuagint as 'pierced' rather than the alternative reading 'like a lion,' a difference of a single letter in the Hebrew, and confirmed by its startling fulfillment in the nail pierced hands and feet of the crucified Christ.

goral.gloss: Lot, a marked object cast to make a decision or division, here used of soldiers dividing a condemned man's clothing, fulfilled precisely at the cross when the Roman soldiers cast lots for Jesus's garment, John 19:23-24.

basic.context: David begins with the rawest possible cry, feeling utterly forsaken by God even while remembering that the fathers before him were never disappointed when they trusted God. He describes being mocked, surrounded like prey by wild animals, his strength failing, his body wasting away. In striking detail he describes his hands and feet being pierced and enemies casting lots for his clothing, images centuries before crucifixion existed as a Roman punishment. Then, without any narrated rescue, the psalm turns completely: David proclaims God's name, and the psalm expands outward until it pictures the whole world, even generations not yet born, turning to worship the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read on two levels held together: it is David's own real experience of suffering and abandonment, expressed in the vivid imagery common to ancient Hebrew poetry, and it is also, by the Spirit's inspiration, genuine prophecy fulfilled with startling precision in the crucifixion of Jesus, who Himself quoted its opening line from the cross. The New Testament treats this psalm as messianic prophecy, not merely as a devotional parallel.
basic.originalLanguages: David's cry uses azab, forsaken, the very word Jesus quotes in Aramaic from the cross. The disputed but well attested reading karah, pierced, in verse 16 anticipates crucifixion centuries before it existed as a punishment, and the casting of goral, lots, for his clothing in verse 18 is fulfilled precisely by the Roman soldiers at the cross.
basic.typology: David's specific suffering, mockery, physical agony, pierced extremities, and divided garments, functions as a detailed prophetic pattern, a type, fulfilled point by point in the crucifixion of Christ, the true sufferer this psalm ultimately describes.
basic.christ: Matthew 27:46 records Jesus quoting this psalm's opening cry word for word from the cross. John 19:23-24 records Roman soldiers casting lots for His garment, fulfilling verse 18. Hebrews 2:12 quotes verse 22, 'I will proclaim Your name to my brothers,' applying it directly to Christ identifying with His people. The psalm's movement from abandonment to worldwide praise mirrors the movement from the cross to the great commission of Matthew 28.
basic.god: God appears here as both hidden, seemingly absent from the sufferer's cry, and as the one who has, in fact, not despised or hidden His face from the afflicted, verse 24, a tension resolved in the cross, where God the Son bears forsakenness so that forsaken sinners might be brought near.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 27:46 records Jesus quoting this psalm's opening words from the cross. John 19:23-24 fulfills the casting of lots for His garment. Hebrews 2:12 quotes verse 22 directly of Christ's identification with His brothers.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's descent into total forsakenness and its ascent into worldwide worship trace the whole gospel story in miniature: Christ bears the full weight of abandonment on the cross so that, through His resurrection, praise for God's righteousness might reach the ends of the earth and generations yet unborn.

context.literary:
Psalm 22 is two psalms joined at one hinge, and the hinge is a single verb. Verses 1 to 21 are a lament, verses 22 to 31 a hymn, and the last line of the lament, 'You have answered me,' verse 21, is what turns one into the other. The Hebrew of that clause is a completed action, not a request. The sufferer has been asking in the present tense for twenty verses, and here, in mid-cry, he reports that the answer has come. The praise that follows is the sound of that discovery.

The lament itself is not one straight line of pain. It moves in three rounds, and each round ends by turning to God. In verses 1 to 5 the sufferer lists his abandonment, then remembers the fathers who trusted and were delivered. In verses 6 to 11 he describes his humiliation, then looks back to his birth, where God was already his God. In verses 12 to 21 the animals close in, and he prays as bluntly as he has complained. Each round pivots on a phrase of the same shape, 'Yet You are holy,' verse 3, 'Yet You brought me forth,' verse 9, and 'But You, O LORD, be not far off,' verse 19. The words 'far' in verses 1, 11 and 19 and 'trust' in verses 4, 5 and 9 give the rounds a shared refrain.

The images escalate by species. First a worm, verse 6, then bulls, verse 12, lions, verse 13, dogs, verse 16 and again in verse 20, and finally the lion and wild oxen together in verse 21. The animals are the sufferer's enemies, and the poet has gathered them from farmyard and wilderness so that nowhere is safe. Beside the animals sits the body, and verses 14 to 17 read like an inventory of failing parts: bones, heart, strength, tongue, hands, feet.

The hymn is built in widening circles. It begins with 'my brothers' and 'the assembly,' verse 22, then widens to those who fear the LORD and all Jacob, verse 23, then to the poor, verse 26, then to the ends of the earth and every family of the nations, verse 27, then even to the dead, 'all who go down to the dust,' verse 29, and last to generations not yet born, verses 30 and 31. The psalm closes on time itself, with the story passed on to a people yet unborn. The final Hebrew word is a verb, 'He has done it.'
context.historical:
The heading ascribes the psalm to David and names a tune, and it names no event. Readers have proposed the years of Saul's pursuit, an illness, or a battle, but the text does not settle it, and the psalm may have been written to be prayed by any sufferer. Its language of animals and bones and thirst is the ordinary vocabulary of lament in the Old Testament, and other psalms use pieces of it: Psalm 31 and Psalm 69 both describe being scorned and thirsty. What is distinctive is the accumulation. No other lament brings so many images of exposure together.

The setting the first hearers would have recognised is the assembly. Verses 22 to 26 describe a public gathering at which the rescued man tells what God did and 'fulfills his vows.' Israel's law provided for exactly this. A person who had been delivered could bring a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and the meat was to be eaten that same day, Leviticus 7:12 and 7:15, which meant the offerer had to share it with others. That is why the poor can 'eat and be satisfied,' verse 26. The psalm is thus not a solitary lament but a lament that ends in a meal, a feast for the poor to celebrate what God has done for one of their own.

Bashan, named in verse 12, was the highland east of the Jordan, famous for its rich pasture and its powerful cattle. Amos 4:1 speaks of 'cows of Bashan,' and Psalm 68:15 calls it 'a mountain of God.' A bull from Bashan was the image of strength that cannot be resisted, so the sufferer's enemies are strong, fed and confident.

The phrase 'I am a worm and not a man' would have struck the first hearers as an extreme self-description. In Isaiah 41:14, God calls Israel 'worm of Jacob' and promises to help, and the word can also name the crimson dye taken from a worm. The sufferer says he is lower than human, and God elsewhere says He comes to just such a creature.

Crucifixion, as the New Testament knows it, was a later Roman practice, and nothing in David's world matches verses 16 to 18 as a legal punishment. The psalm's physical images are the language of a man who is hunted, wasted and stripped. They were understood in Israel as poetry of extremity, and only in retrospect did the church see how closely they fit the cross.
context.canonical:
Psalm 22 stands in the middle of a deliberate sequence. Psalm 20 was a prayer for the king, Psalm 21 the thanksgiving for his crown, and Psalm 22 opens with the same kind of figure in unbearable abandonment. Psalm 23 follows with the Shepherd, and Psalm 24 with the King entering the gates. The order can be heard as cross, shepherd, enthronement, though the psalms were arranged by editors who did not need the New Testament to see the shape. What they knew was that a suffering that ends in praise is a pattern the whole Psalter follows.

The opening cry belongs to a family of lament that asks 'why.' Psalm 88:14 asks, 'Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?' and Psalm 44 says to God that 'You have rejected and humbled us,' verse 9. These are honest prayers of the faithful. Psalm 22 stands apart from them because it also moves out of the pit into praise and then keeps widening, until the verdict on the sufferer becomes a message for the nations.

The psalm is caught up with the Servant of Isaiah 53. The Servant is 'oppressed and afflicted,' Isaiah 53:7, 'pierced for our transgressions,' Isaiah 53:5, and then 'will see His offspring' and 'prolong His days,' Isaiah 53:10, which matches the psalm's movement from the dust of death to a posterity that serves Him, verse 30. Isaiah 49:6 adds the widening of the mission, 'a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth,' which is where verse 27 ends.

In the New Testament the psalm lies under the whole passion. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John each use it. The Gospels use its opening cry, Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34, the mockery, Matthew 27:39 to 43, and the garments, Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34 and John 19:23 to 24. John also marks thirst, 'I am thirsty,' John 19:28, and the psalm's 'my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth' lies close by, although John names Psalm 69:21 in the background. Hebrews 2:11 to 13 then takes verse 22 and puts it in the mouth of the risen Christ speaking of His people as brothers.

Luke 24:44 says that everything written about Christ 'in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms' must be fulfilled, and Psalm 22 is one of the clearest cases. It is worth noting that the New Testament does not treat all of it as prediction. It hears the psalm as the prayer of a righteous sufferer whose story a greater sufferer takes up and completes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The first hearers were meant to learn that a person can say to God what verses 1 and 2 say and still be inside the faith. The psalm begins with 'My God, my God,' so the cry of abandonment is addressed to the One who has abandoned him, which is an act of faith as well as of pain. The author gives Israel words for the darkest nights, and he does not soften them.

He also means the hearers to notice that the sufferer does not stay at the level of feeling. In verses 3 to 5 he corrects his own experience by telling himself the history of Israel: the fathers trusted and were delivered. In verses 9 and 10 he tells himself his own history, that God has held him since birth. The point is that faith argues with feeling by recalling what God has done, and the psalm gives the worshipper a script for that argument.

Verse 24 is the theological centre of the second half. The lament had said that God does not answer, verse 2, and the hymn now says that He 'has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.' The author wants the hearers to trust the second statement over the first. God's silence was real in experience, but it was not the truth about God, and Israel is invited to say so aloud in the assembly.

The hymn's widening circles carry another purpose. The private sufferer's rescue is not a private matter, and it becomes the ground on which the nations turn to the LORD. The author wants Israel to see that God's dealings with a single afflicted person are the way He advertises His kingship, verse 28. A worshipper who has been through such an ordeal is to tell the story, because it is the means by which a people not yet born will come to know God's righteousness, verse 31.

Finally, the psalm means to hold out hope past death. Verse 29 imagines even the dying kneeling before the LORD, and verse 26 says 'May your hearts live forever.' Israel's hope was not yet spelled out, but the author places it here, in the assembly of the redeemed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records one man's suffering and rescue, and it does not lay down a rule for how every believer will suffer. Nothing in it says that faithful people will always be mocked, or that a rescue always arrives before the end. Reading the psalm as a promise that every persecuted believer will be delivered would run against the rest of the Bible, where the faithful sometimes die in the middle of the story, Hebrews 11:35 to 38. The psalm describes what happened to this sufferer, and the New Testament tells us what happened to Jesus.

It is also a description, not a command, to feel forsaken. Verse 1 is not a call to doubt; it is a permitted way of praying when doubt comes. The psalm's prescriptive weight lies in what the sufferer does with the feeling: he keeps addressing God, he rehearses God's past faithfulness, he prays for help, and he vows to praise. Those verbs are what carry over to us.

There is a quieter matter of interpretation. The psalm's account of Jesus on the cross should not be turned into a checklist of prophecy, as though every phrase had a matching event. The New Testament itself picks out a few, the cry, the mockery, the garments, the thirst and the brothers, and it never says that the bulls, the lions or the dogs are meant as coded soldiers. The church is on firmer ground when it says that the psalm was David's prayer, and the same words, prayed by the Son, were filled beyond anything David could have imagined.

Finally, the second half is prescriptive for congregations. A person who has been delivered is expected to tell it, vow and feast with the poor, verses 22 to 26, and the church still gathers to do this.

debates.question: Did David experience what verses 14 to 18 describe, or is this suffering beyond his own history?

views.label: Hebrew lament poetry, spoken in extreme images, that finds its literal fulfilment only in Christ
views.case: No account of David's life records his hands and feet being pierced or his clothes shared out by lot. The images are drawn from the vocabulary of hunted men, and the language of animals and bones is figurative. On this view the psalm's specific force came to light when the Gospels described the cross, and the New Testament writers read it backwards.

views.label: David's real suffering, prayed in words the Spirit prepared for a greater sufferer
views.case: The psalm gives no sign of being written by someone else about someone else, since it is in the first person and is a genuine cry. The words of the psalm were David's prayer in a real crisis, and they were also, by the Spirit's design, framed to hold the passion of Christ. Peter speaks in this way of David as a prophet in Acts 2:30.

views.label: A typical righteous sufferer, David as the pattern of every afflicted king
views.case: Some see David as the representative of the anointed king who suffers and is delivered. His experience is the type, and Christ, as the greater Son of David, is its complete case. The psalm does not need to be exact autobiography to be true of him.

debates.bearing: On every view Jesus prays these words as His own and lives them out, and the church has always heard David's voice and Christ's voice in the same psalm.

debates.question: How should the disputed word in verse 16 be read?

views.label: 'They have pierced my hands and feet' (the reading of the Dead Sea Scrolls and the ancient versions)
views.case: The BSB footnote says that the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac support 'pierced.' The Septuagint has the Greek translators write that they 'dug' the hands and feet, which is the same idea. The reading also gives the verse a verb where the other reading leaves the sentence incomplete, and it fits the crucifixion sight.

views.label: 'Like a lion at my hands and feet' (the reading of most Masoretic manuscripts)
views.case: Most Hebrew manuscripts read a form that means 'like a lion.' The Hebrew for 'lion' and the verb differ by one small letter, so a copyist could easily have mistaken one for the other. Those who keep the Masoretic reading point out that the lions of verses 13 and 21 make it thematically natural. Even so, the verse's grammar has to be stretched, since a verb is missing.

debates.bearing: Even if one prefers the lion reading, the New Testament does not rest its case on verse 16. It cites the garments in verse 18, the mockery in verse 8 and the cry in verse 1, and none of them depends on this one word.

debates.question: What explains the sudden turn at verse 22?

views.label: A priestly or prophetic word of assurance spoken between the two halves
views.case: Some suppose that in the temple a priest or prophet spoke an oracle of salvation after the lament, which the psalm leaves unwritten. The change from complaint to praise between verses 21 and 22 is then explained by a silent word from God. Other psalms show such shifts, and Psalm 12:5 gives an actual divine word inside a lament.

views.label: The sufferer's own report that he has been answered
views.case: The final clause of verse 21, 'You have answered me,' reads as the sufferer's own announcement. The answer has come, in whatever form, and the praise is the response. The turn is abrupt only because the psalm does not narrate the deliverance, but it does state it.

debates.bearing: Both views say the same at the pastoral level: the praise does not rest on the sufferer's feelings improving but on God's having heard, and the psalm teaches worshippers to move toward that certainty.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean by quoting the first line of the psalm?

views.label: He was actually forsaken as He bore sin
views.case: Paul says that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that Christ became 'a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. On this reading the cry is real: the Son experienced the loss of the Father's face that belongs to sin's judgment. Many Reformers, Calvin among them, taught this.

views.label: He was praying the whole psalm, which ends in vindication
views.case: It is argued that a first line could stand for a whole psalm, and that a person praying Psalm 22 in agony was also praying its ending. On this reading the cry is a declaration of trust as much as pain, and His last words from Psalm 31:5, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' point the same way, Luke 23:46.

views.label: Both, since the cry can be real and the psalm can be whole
views.case: Jesus can quote a psalm that includes both abandonment and praise because His experience contains both. The cry expresses the actual weight, while the psalm places that weight inside a trust that does not let go of 'My God.' This reading holds the two things together and does not have to choose.

debates.bearing: The New Testament does not say the Father stopped being His Father, and it does not say the cry was play-acting. The safest course is to say that the cry was real and that the trust was real.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 has two words that repay attention beyond the 'forsaken' the basic level names. The 'words of groaning' are literally 'the words of my roaring,' from a noun that describes the sound of a lion, and Psalm 32:3 uses the same word for the sufferer's 'groaning all day long' when he kept silent about his sin. The sound the psalm describes is not polite prayer but a roar. The verb translated 'far' in 'so far from saving me' is the adjective rachoq, and it recurs in verses 11 and 19, so that the plea 'be not far' is the psalm's request in the middle and at the end.

Verse 3 calls God 'holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel.' The Hebrew is 'You sit, enthroned' with the object 'the praises,' and it presents Israel's worship as the seat on which God takes His place among His people. The lament is thus held up against a God whose habit is to be praised, and the sufferer implicitly asks how a God enthroned on praise can be silent to a man who is praising.

In verse 6 'worm' is tola'at, the crimson worm from which red dye was made. The same Hebrew word is also the common word for crimson, and the sufferer chooses the smallest and most crushable of creatures to describe himself. The word appears again in Isaiah 41:14, where God addresses Israel as 'worm of Jacob' and promises help.

Verses 9 and 10 use two verbs about birth. The first says that God 'brought me forth' from the womb, which is a midwife's word, and the second, 'cast upon You,' from the root shalak, says the child was thrown onto God's arms at birth as onto a parent. The verse insists that the sufferer never had a moment without God, which is why the silence of verse 2 hurts so much.

In verse 16 the reading discussed in the debate turns on a single small letter, and the BSB footnote records that the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac support 'pierced.' It is honest to say that the reading is textually contested even though it is well attested. The word for 'dogs' in verses 16 and 20 is kelavim, unclean scavengers, and the phrase 'wild dogs' in the BSB of verse 20 is the noun for dogs again. The 'precious life' of verse 20 is literally 'my only one,' yechidah, the word used of Isaac in Genesis 22:2, 'your only son.' The sufferer's life is the only one he has, and it is so valuable that it is like an only child.

Verse 21's 'You have answered me' is the psalm's hinge. The verb is a completed action, anitani, 'You have answered me.' It follows a run of imperatives, 'Deliver,' 'Save,' and it introduces verse 22, where the sufferer at once turns to the assembly.

In verse 26 the phrase 'May your hearts live forever' changes the address, so that the sufferer now speaks to the poor in the second person. The verb 'live' is the plain word chayah, and the wish is for a life that outlasts the meal.

In verse 27 the nations 'will remember and turn to the LORD,' yizkeru and yashuvu. To 'remember' here is an act of the will, not of memory only, and to 'turn' is the usual word for repentance. The kingdom of verse 28 is the Hebrew melukhah, the word Obadiah 1:21 uses when the prophet says that 'the kingdom will belong to the LORD.'

Verses 30 and 31 speak of a 'seed' who serves and a people 'yet unborn,' am nolad, which recalls Psalm 102:18, 'a people not yet created.' The psalm ends on a verb, 'He has done it.'

typology.fulfillment: The sufferer's enemies shake their heads and sneer, 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him.' At the cross the passers-by 'heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads,' Matthew 27:39, and the chief priests said, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43. The BSB footnote to verse 8 marks the citation. The correspondence is remarkable, and the escalation lies in what the mockers meant as taunt: the Son really did trust the Father, and God did deliver Him, on the third day. The type falls short in that David's mockers were not blaspheming God's Son.

typology.type: The garments divided by lot, verse 18
typology.fulfillment: The stripped sufferer watches his clothing shared out. The soldiers at the cross 'divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier,' and cast lots for the seamless tunic, and John says, 'This was to fulfill the Scripture,' John 19:23 to 24. All four Gospels mention the lots, and Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24 and Luke 23:34 record it. The correspondence is exact, and the escalation is that what was a poet's picture of disgrace becomes the sign that the sufferer is Jesus. The type falls short in that we cannot say David lost his clothes in this way.

typology.type: Thirst and the dust of death, verses 14 and 15
typology.fulfillment: The sufferer is 'poured out like water,' his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth, and God lays him 'in the dust of death.' John records Jesus saying 'I am thirsty,' John 19:28, and the burial that follows, verses 38 to 42, brings Him into the dust in earnest. The psalm says that God lays the sufferer there, which matches Peter's word that Christ's death was 'the deliberate plan and foreknowledge of God,' Acts 2:23. The type falls short because David's dust was a metaphor for near death, while Christ's was a tomb.

typology.type: The brothers and the assembly, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: After the cry, the sufferer says he will proclaim God's name 'to my brothers.' Hebrews 2:11 to 12 puts this in the mouth of Jesus: 'Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. He says: I will proclaim Your name to My brothers.' The escalation is that the brothers are all whom He sanctifies, made one family with Him. Israel's assembly becomes the church. The type falls short because David's brothers were fellow Israelites, while Christ's are drawn from every nation.

typology.type: The nations who remember and turn, verses 27 to 28
typology.fulfillment: The sufferer's rescue draws 'all the ends of the earth' to the LORD. After the resurrection the risen Jesus says, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:18 to 19. John sees 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9. The correspondence is between the psalm's widening circles and the Great Commission. The type falls short in that the psalm does not yet say how the nations will hear, and the New Testament supplies the answer of a gospel carried by the church.

study.christ:
Psalm 22 leads to Christ more directly than almost any other psalm, and the New Testament shows how. The Gospels put the opening line on His lips, Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34, and they set the mockery, the garments and the thirst around it. But the link is deeper than a set of matching details. The psalm shapes the whole passion narrative: Jesus dies as a righteous man who trusted God, who was scorned for that trust, and who now prays a prayer of trust in the darkness. The mockers unknowingly quote verse 8, and the words 'He trusts in God' are the truest thing said about Him that day.

Christ enters the psalm as the sufferer, and the Christian reader must let the cry mean what it says. Paul says that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that He 'became a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The cry of verse 1 is what that looks like from the inside: the Son takes on Himself the abandonment that belongs to sin. The psalm makes room for that reading because its sufferer is not a sinner protesting his punishment but an innocent man who cannot find his God.

The psalm also shows the other side of the cry. Luke records Jesus dying with 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, a line from Psalm 31:5. Between 'My God' at the ninth hour and 'Father' at the end, the same Man holds the two prayers together. Hebrews says that in His earthly days He 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard,' Hebrews 5:7. The answer of verse 21 is fulfilled when He is raised.

The second half is Christ's as well, and Hebrews 2 shows it. The writer says that Jesus, having been made perfect through suffering, 'is not ashamed to call them brothers,' and then quotes verse 22 as the Lord's own voice: 'I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly,' Hebrews 2:10 to 12. The risen Christ is the one who leads the congregation's praise. Every hymn the church sings is sung with Him.

The widening circles of verses 27 to 31 lead to the Great Commission and beyond it to the multitude of Revelation 7:9. The suffering of one Man becomes the news that brings the nations. Verse 31, 'He has done it,' has been heard by many readers behind John's 'It is finished,' John 19:30, although John does not quote the psalm there.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm was David's prayer first, and it should not be flattened into a script for Good Friday. Nor should we treat every phrase as a hidden picture of Jesus: the bulls of Bashan are not soldiers in disguise. The New Testament chooses its citations, and we can rest on those it chooses and on the psalm's shape, in which a righteous sufferer is heard and a worldwide people are gathered.
study.god:
The psalm's first lesson about God is that He can be experienced as absent without being absent. The sufferer says twice that God does not answer, verses 1 and 2, and says that God is 'far,' verses 1, 11 and 19. The psalm never denies the experience. Yet verse 24 declares that God 'has not hidden His face from him.' What the psalm holds together is the truth that the sufferer's experience of silence is real and that his God has been listening all the while. This is a tension that God does not resolve by explaining it but by delivering.

God is holy and He is enthroned on praise, verse 3. Holiness here does not put God at a distance from the sufferer. The sufferer takes it as a reason to ask: since God is holy, His character does not change, and what He did for the fathers He can do again. The doctrine of divine holiness in this psalm serves the afflicted.

God is the God of birth and beginnings. Verses 9 and 10 name Him as the One who drew the child from the womb and secured him at the breast. The Creator who made a person is not indifferent to what becomes of him, and the psalm puts that memory in the mouth of a man who now feels dropped. It teaches worshippers to pray from the beginning of the story, not only from the present moment.

God is King. The heart of the second half is verse 28, 'dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations.' Suffering that seems to say that the world is out of control is answered by a declaration that God's rule is not in question. The reach of that rule takes in the rich and the dying, verse 29, and generations not yet born, verses 30 and 31. There is no class of person the LORD does not claim.

God is on the side of the afflicted. Verse 24 says that He 'has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted,' and the poor are given a feast, verse 26. God's kingship is exercised in mercy to the low.

The cross brings a further and deeper truth. Christian theology has taught that the Son bore forsakenness for us, and that God the Father did not cease to be His Father. The Reformers spoke of Jesus tasting the wrath due to sin. We must avoid saying that the Trinity was torn, since Scripture says that 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself,' 2 Corinthians 5:19, and Hebrews says that Christ 'through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14. What Psalm 22 provides is the grammar of the event: a real cry, a real answer, and a God who is not less good for allowing the darkness.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to pray honestly, to remember God's history, and to tell the story of rescue to the assembly. It invites the church to sing with the risen Christ, and it places the poor at the feast.

crossReferences.note: The passers-by shake their heads and the chief priests say, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him.' The words are close to Psalm 22:7 to 8. The mockers unwittingly play the part of the psalm's enemies, and the psalm gives the reader the frame in which to see the scene.

Mark gives the cry in its Aramaic form, 'Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani,' and translates it. Preserving the sounds of the moment shows that early Christians treasured the very words. It is the only saying of Jesus from the cross that Mark records in words.

The soldiers do not tear the seamless tunic but cast lots for it, and John says this fulfilled the Scripture. He quotes Psalm 22:18 in full. The scene shows how exactly a poet's image of shared-out clothing fitted what the soldiers actually did.

Knowing that everything had been accomplished, Jesus says 'I am thirsty,' and then 'It is finished.' The thirst is close to Psalm 22:15, and the closing 'It is finished' may echo the psalm's last word, 'He has done it.' John does not quote the psalm here, so the echo is a matter of resonance.

The writer puts Psalm 22:22 in the mouth of Christ: 'I will proclaim Your name to My brothers.' Because the One who sanctifies and those He sanctifies share one family, He is not ashamed of them. The passage turns the psalm's second half into the risen Lord's own praise among the church.

Jesus dies with 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' from Psalm 31:5. The Gospel writer sets it against the cry of Psalm 22:1. Between the two, the same voice moves from the darkness of 'My God' to the trust of 'Father,' and the pair shows how the psalms shaped His dying.

The Servant is pierced, crushed and silent, and 'led like a lamb to the slaughter.' The Servant Song and the psalm share a sufferer who is innocent, scorned and finally vindicated. Read together they show that Israel's Scriptures already held the shape of a righteous one who suffers for others.

God says, 'They will look on Me, the One they have pierced,' and mourning follows. It speaks of a pierced figure and shares the language of Psalm 22:16 and the piercing at the cross. John 19:37 quotes this text of the spear thrust, so the two witnesses meet in the same scene.

'Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?' Psalm 88 has the same question as Psalm 22:1 and none of Psalm 22's turn to praise. The Psalter keeps both, so that a reader whose night has not ended is not made to feel that faith has failed.

God says, 'In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you.' It states the pattern of Psalm 22: the hidden face is for a moment, the kindness is everlasting, and verse 24 says the face was not hidden in the end.

'Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD.' It shares the aim of Psalm 22:30 to 31, that a story of affliction and rescue is told to those unborn. Both psalms treat their words as an inheritance.

A multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' stands before the Lamb. It is the fulfilment of the widening circles of Psalm 22:27, where the ends of the earth remember and every family bows. The crowd exists because the Lamb was slain.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 22 answers a question that the earlier story has left hanging: what does God do with an innocent sufferer? Genesis 3 had said that a woman's seed would be bruised in the heel, and Genesis 4 showed Abel's blood crying from the ground. Job asked why the righteous suffer. The Psalms carry the question in their laments, and here is a psalm that says that the suffering of the righteous is not the last word, and that the last word is praise, first in the assembly and then among the nations.

It looks back to the promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, because verse 27 speaks of 'all the families of the nations' bowing before the LORD. The shape of the psalm, one afflicted man and then a world, is the shape of Abraham's story compressed. It also recalls the exodus, since verses 4 and 5 rest on the fathers who 'cried out to You and were set free,' the same verb as in Exodus 2:23, and this psalm asks whether the God who heard Israel in Egypt will hear one man now.

It sets up the Servant of Isaiah, who is pierced and crushed and then sees offspring, Isaiah 53, and it sets up the Christ of the Gospels, who prays its opening words in the dark. In the passion, everything the psalm holds in poetic tension is lived out in a single day: the mockery, the shared clothing, the thirst, the dust, and the cry. The Gospels then record the answer of verse 21 in the resurrection, and Hebrews places verse 22 on the risen Christ's lips.

The middle of the story is therefore this: at the cross Christ takes the abandonment that belongs to sinners, and through it He opens the way for forsaken people to be brought near. Paul says 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?' Romans 8:32. The circle of praise then widens through the church, Matthew 28:19, and no one is left outside its reach.

The new creation is the psalm's final line lived out. John sees a crowd from every nation before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 7:9, and hears that 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15. The poor eat and are satisfied, and the hungry will hunger no more, Revelation 7:16. The generations not yet born have been born, and they tell what He has done.

sermon.title: Make Me Understand It!
sermon.why: Begg considers this psalm in light of its ultimate fulfillment in the Lord Jesus, who was rejected by men and bore the wrath of God in the place of sinners, showing that only through trusting in Christ's substitutionary death can sinners enjoy a restored relationship with God.

quiz.q: Where does the New Testament directly quote this psalm's opening cry?

options.text: Jesus quotes it word for word from the cross in Matthew 27:46, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken Me?'
options.note: This is one of the most direct and significant quotations of an Old Testament psalm in all four Gospels' passion narratives.

options.text: Paul quotes it in his letter to the Romans regarding justification.
options.note: The direct quotation of this exact cry appears in Matthew's crucifixion account, not in Romans.

options.text: It is quoted by John the Baptist at Jesus's baptism.
options.note: This psalm's cry is quoted at the crucifixion, not at the baptism narrative.

options.text: It is never directly quoted in the New Testament.
options.note: This is incorrect; it is quoted directly and prominently in Matthew 27:46.

quiz.q: What specific detail in verse 16 anticipates crucifixion centuries before it existed as a punishment?

options.text: The piercing of hands and feet.
options.note: This detail, confirmed by ancient translations and fulfilled at the cross, is remarkable given crucifixion was not yet practiced when the psalm was written.

options.text: The mention of a crown of thorns.
options.note: The crown of thorns is a separate detail from the Gospel accounts, not found in this specific psalm.

options.text: A description of being buried in a borrowed tomb.
options.note: The burial detail comes from Isaiah 53, not from this specific verse in Psalm 22.

options.text: The exact number of lashes given before crucifixion.
options.note: This psalm does not specify a number of lashes; its precise, striking detail is the piercing of hands and feet.

quiz.q: What happens with the sufferer's garments in verse 18, and how is it fulfilled?

options.text: His garments are divided and lots are cast for his clothing, fulfilled precisely when Roman soldiers cast lots for Jesus's garment, John 19:23-24.
options.note: This is one of the most precise and historically documented fulfillments of Old Testament prophecy in the New Testament.

options.text: His garments are given away willingly as gifts to his followers.
options.note: The psalm describes enemies dividing and casting lots for garments, not the sufferer willingly giving gifts.

options.text: His garments are burned in judgment.
options.note: The text describes division and casting lots, not burning.

options.text: The psalm makes no mention of the sufferer's garments.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly addresses the division of garments and casting of lots.

quiz.q: How does the psalm's mood shift between verses 21 and 22?

options.text: It moves, without any narrated resolution, from desperate cries for rescue to confident proclamation of God's name and praise.
options.note: This abrupt but complete turn is one of the most striking features of the psalm's structure.

options.text: It moves from praise back into deeper despair with no resolution at all.
options.note: This reverses the actual direction of the psalm, which moves from despair toward praise, not the other way around.

options.text: The mood remains identical throughout the entire psalm with no shift.
options.note: The shift between the first and second halves of the psalm is one of its most notable and widely discussed features.

options.text: It shifts from praise to a detailed description of a specific military battle.
options.note: The shift is from lament to worship and worldwide praise, not to a military battle narrative.

quiz.q: What is the scope of the praise described in the psalm's closing verses, 27-31?

options.text: It reaches to all the ends of the earth, all the families of the nations, and a people yet unborn.
options.note: This expansive, worldwide, and even future generational scope mirrors the global reach of the gospel after Christ's resurrection.

options.text: It is limited strictly to the immediate members of David's own household.
options.note: The text explicitly expands to all the ends of the earth and generations yet unborn, far beyond David's household.

options.text: It applies only to the priestly tribe of Levi.
options.note: The scope described is universal, all nations and unborn generations, not limited to a single tribe.

options.text: It is restricted to a single future military victory.
options.note: The praise described is worship and proclamation of God's righteousness, not a military victory account.

questions: Jesus quoted this psalm's opening cry from the cross, entering fully into the experience of feeling forsaken. Does knowing that Christ Himself voiced this exact cry change how you bring your own feelings of God's absence to Him honestly?

The sufferer remembers that the fathers before him trusted and were never disappointed, even while his own present experience feels like abandonment. How do you hold together remembered faithfulness and present distress when God feels far away?
The mockers in this psalm taunt, 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him', words nearly repeated at the cross. Have you ever faced mockery for your faith, and how did you respond?

This psalm moves, without any narrated explanation, from utter despair to worldwide praise. Where in your own life have you experienced or hoped for that kind of unexplained turn from despair toward praise?

The psalm's closing vision reaches to a people yet unborn proclaiming God's righteousness. How does being part of that same ongoing story, generations still coming to praise God because of Christ, shape the way you think about your own part in passing on faith to others?

translationNotes.note: Pierced renders a Hebrew reading, karu, attested by the Septuagint and other ancient witnesses, differing by a single letter from an alternative reading sometimes rendered 'like a lion'; the piercing reading is strongly supported and finds a striking fulfillment in the crucifixion.

The casting of lots for the sufferer's garment is fulfilled precisely and historically by the Roman soldiers at the crucifixion, John 19:23-24, one of the New Testament's clearest direct fulfillments of psalm prophecy.
